source_text: Ην ἄρα, ὡς ἔοικεν, πάντων μέγιστον μαθημάτων τὸ γνῶναι αὑτόν· ἑαυτὸν γάρ τις ἐὰν γνῷ, θεὸν εἴσεται, θεὸν δὲ εἰδὼς ἐξομοιωθήσεται θεῷ, οὐ χρυσοφορῶν οὐδὲ ποδηροφορῶν, ἀλλὰ ἀγαθοεργῶν καὶ ὅτι μάλιστα ὀλιγίστων δεόμενος· ἀνενδεὴς δὲ μόνος ὁ θεὸς καὶ χαίρει μάλιστα μὲν καθαρεύοντας ἡμᾶς ὁρῶν τῷ τῆς διανοίας κόσμῳ, ἔπειτα δὲ καὶ τῷ τοῦ σώματος, ἁγνὴν στολήν, σωφροσύνην, περιβεβλημένους. τριγενοῦς οὖν ὑπαρχούσης τῆς ψυχῆς τὸ νοερόν, ὅ δὴ λογιστικὸν καλεῖται, ὁ ἄνθρωπός ἐστιν ὁ ἔνδον, ὁ τοῦ φαινομένου τοῦδε ἄρχων ἀνθρώπου, αὐτὸν δὲ ἐκεῖνον ἄλλος ἄγει, θεός· τὸ δὲ θυμικόν, θηριῶδες ὄν, πλησίον μανίας οἰκεῖ· πολύμορφον δὲ τὸ ἐπιθυμητικὸν καὶ τρίτον, ὑπὲρ τὸν Πρωτέα τὸν θαλάττιον δαίμονα ποικίλον, ἄλλοτε ἄλλως μετασχηματιζόμενον, εἰς μοιχείας καὶ λαγνείας καὶ εἰς φθορὰς ἐξαρεσκευόμενον· ἤτοι μὲν πρώτιστα λέων γένετ᾿ ἠυγένειος, ἔτι φέρων τὸν καλλωπισμόν· ἄνδρα δείκνυσιν ἡ τοῦ γενείου κόμη· αὐτὰρ ἔπειτα δράκων ἢ πάρδαλις ἠδὲ μέγας σῦς· κατώλισθεν εἰς τὴν ἀσέλγειαν ἡ φιλοκοσμία. οὐκέτι καρτερῷ θηρίῳ † ἄνθρωπος φαίνεται, γίνετο δ᾿ ὑγρὸν ὕδωρ καὶ δένδρεον ὑψιπέτηλον. ἐκχεῖται τὰ πάθη, ἐκβλύζονται αἱ ἡδοναί, μαραίνεται τὸ κάλλος, καὶ θᾶττον ἀποπίπτει τοῦ πετάλου χαμαί, ὅταν αὐτοῦ καταπνεύσωσιν αἱ ἐρωτικαὶ τῆς ὕβρεως λαίλαπες, καὶ πρὶν ἢ τὸ μετόπωρον ἐλθεῖν μαραίνεται τῇ φθορᾷ· πάντα γὰρ ἡ ἐπιθυμία γίνεταί τε καὶ πλάττεται καὶ φενακίζειν βούλεται, ἵνα κατακρύψῃ τὸν ἄνθρωπον. ὁ δὲ ἄνθρωπος ἐκεῖνος, ᾧ σύνοικος ὁ λόγος, οὐ ποικίλλεται, οὐ πλάττεται, μορφὴν ἔχει τὴν τοῦ λόγου, ἐξομοιοῦται τῷ θεῷ, καλός ἐστιν, οὐ καλλωπίζεται· κάλλος ἐστὶ τὸ ἀληθινόν, καὶ γὰρ ὁ θεός ἐστιν· θεὸς δὲ ἐκεῖνος ὁ ἄνθρωπος γίνεται, ὅτι βούλεται ὃ θεός. ὀρθῶς ἄρα εἶπεν Ἡράκλειτος· »ἄνθρωποι θεοί, θεοὶ ἄνθρωποι. λόγος γὰρ ωὐτός·« μυστήριον ἐμφανές· θεὸς ἐν ἀνθρώπῳ, καὶ ὁ ἄνθρωπος θεός, καὶ τὸ θέλημα τοῦ πατρὸς ὁ μεσίτης ἐκτελεῖ· μεσίτης γὰρ ὁ λόγος ὁ κοινὸς ἀμφοῖν, θεοῦ μὲν υἱός, σωτὴρ δὲ ἀνθρώπων, καὶ τοῦ μὲν διάκονος, ἡμῶν δὲ παιδαγωγός. δούλης δὲ οὔσης τῆς σαρκός, καθὼς καὶ ὁ Παῦλος μαρτυρεῖ, πῶς ἄν τις εἰκότως τὴν θεράπαιναν κοσμοίη προαγωγοῦ δίκην; ὅτι γὰρ δούλου μορφὴ τὸ σαρκικόν, ἐπὶ τοῦ κυρίου φησὶν ὁ ἀπόστολος· »ὅτι ἐκένωσεν ἑαυτὸν μορφὴν δούλου λαβών«, τὸν ἐκτὸς ἄνθρωπον δοῦλον προσειπὼν πρὶν ἢ δουλεῦσαι καὶ σαρκοφορῆσαι τὸν κύριον. ὁ δὲ συμπαθὴς θεὸς αὐτὸς ἠλευθέρωσεν τὴν σάρκα τῆς φθορᾶς καὶ δουλείας τῆς θανατηφόρου καὶ πικρᾶς ἀπαλλάξας τὴν ἀφθαρσίαν περιέθηκεν αὐτῇ, ἅγιον τοῦτο τῇ σαρκὶ [καὶ] ἀιδιότητος καλλώπισμα περιθείς, τὴν ἀθανασίαν. ἔστι δὲ καὶ ἄλλο κάλλος ἀνθρώπων ἀγάπη· »ἀγάπη δέ«, κατὰ τὸν ἀπόστολον, »μακροθυμεῖ, χρηστεύεται, οὐ ζηλοῖ, οὐ περπερεύεται, οὐ φυσιοῦται.« περπερεία γὰρ ὁ καλλωπισμὸς περιττότητος καὶ ἀχρειότητος ἔχων ἔμφασιν. διὸ καὶ ἐπιφέρει· »οὐκ ἀσχημονεῖ.« ἄσχημον γὰρ τὸ ἀλλότριον καὶ μὴ κατὰ φύσιν σχῆμα· τὸ δ᾿ ἐπίπλαστον ἀλλότριον, ὅπερ ἐξηγεῖται σαφῶς, »οὐ ζητεῖ« φήσας »τὸ μὴ ἑαυτῆς«· τὸ γὰρ ἴδιον ἡ ἀλήθεια τὸ οἰκεῖον καλεῖ, τὸ δ᾿ ἀλλότριον ἡ φιλοκοσμία ζητεῖ, ἐκτὸς οὖσα καὶ τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ τοῦ λόγου καὶ τῆς ἀγάπης. τὸν δὲ κύριον αὐτὸν τὴν ὄψιν αἰσχρὸν γεγονέναι διὰ Ἡσαΐου τὸ πνεῦμα μαρτυρεῖ· »καὶ εἴδομεν αὐτόν, καὶ οὐκ εἶχεν εἶδος οὐδὲ κάλλος, ἀλλὰ τὸ εἶδος αὐτοῦ ἄτιμον, ἐκλεῖπον παρὰ τοὺς ἀνθρώπους.« καὶ τίς ἀμείνων κυρίου; ἀλλ᾿ οὐ τὸ κάλλος τῆς σαρκὸς τὸ φαντασιαστικόν, τὸ δὲ ἀληθινὸν καὶ τῆς ψυχῆς καὶ τοῦ σώματος ἐνεδείξατο κάλλος, τῆς μὲν τὸ εὐεργετικόν, τὸ δὲ ἀθάνατον τῆς σαρκός.
pass_a_gloss: It was, therefore, as it seems, the greatest of lessons to know oneself; for if someone knows himself, he will also know God, and knowing God, he will be made like God, not by wearing gold or walking in fancy shoes, but by doing good and needing the least, for only God is without need and He is delighted, seeing us being purified in the adornment of the mind, and then also in the body, having put on the pure garment, self-control, and modesty. Since the soul has a threefold existence, the rational part, which is called the logical, is the inner man, the ruler of the visible man, and this man is led by another, God; the passionate part, being beast-like, is near to madness; the desiring part, being multiform and more varied than the sea-demon Proteus, is transformed in various ways, being led to adulteries and lusts and corruptions; at one time it becomes a lion, still wearing its beautiful appearance, showing the hair of its kind; then it becomes a dragon or a leopard or a large pig; the love of beauty has fallen into shamelessness. The man is no longer seen as a strong animal, but becomes liquid water and a tall tree; the passions are poured out, the pleasures are spilled, beauty withers, and it quickly falls from its petal to the ground when the erotic blasts of insolence blow on it, and it withers away with corruption before the afternoon comes; for all things are done and formed and pretended by desire, so that it may hide the man. But the man who has the Word dwelling with him does not change, is not formed, has the form of the Word, is made like God, is beautiful, not adorned with beauty; beauty is the true thing, and God is; and that man becomes God, because he wills what God wills. Heraclitus spoke rightly: 'men are gods, gods are men', a clear mystery; God is in man, and man is God, and the will of the Father is carried out by the Mediator; for the Word is the common Mediator of both, the Son of God and the Savior of men, and the servant of God and the Pedagogue of men. But since the flesh is a slave, as Paul also testifies, how can one reasonably adorn the servant like a leader? For the apostle says that the fleshly thing is the form of a slave, saying 'he emptied himself, taking the form of a slave'; he calls the outer man a slave before the Lord became a slave and wore flesh. But the sympathetic God Himself freed the flesh from corruption and the slavery of death-bearing and bitter things, and having taken away corruption, He put on it the incorruptibility, the adornment of immortality. And there is also another beauty of men, love; 'for love', according to the apostle, 'is patient, is kind, does not envy, does not boast, is not puffed up'; for boasting is the adornment of excess and uselessness, having emphasis. Therefore, he also adds 'it does not behave shamefully'; for what is foreign and not according to nature is shameful; what is added is foreign, which he explains clearly, saying 'it does not seek what is not its own'; for truth calls its own thing its own, but the love of beauty seeks what is foreign, being outside of God and the Word and love. And the Spirit testifies through Isaiah that the Lord Himself became unattractive in appearance; 'and we saw Him, and He had no form or beauty, but His appearance was without honor, despised by men'. And who is better than the Lord? But not the imaginary beauty of the flesh, but the true beauty of the soul and the body, which He showed, the beneficial one of the soul and the immortal one of the flesh.

pass_b_english: It seems that the greatest of all lessons is to know oneself; for if someone comes to know himself, he will also know God, and knowing God, he will be made like God—not by wearing gold or walking in fancy shoes, but by doing good and needing the very least, since only God is without need. He delights most of all when He sees us being purified in the adornment of the mind, and then also in the body, clothed with the pure garment of self-control and modesty. Because the soul has a threefold nature, the rational part—what we call the logical faculty—is the inner man, the ruler of this visible man, and this inner man is guided by another: God. The passionate part, being beast-like, dwells near madness. The desiring part is multiform, more varied than the sea-demon Proteus, shifting into one shape after another, drawn toward adulteries, lusts, and corruptions. At one moment it becomes a noble lion, still wearing its beauty, its mane proclaiming its kind; then it becomes a dragon or a leopard or a great boar; love of beauty has fallen into shamelessness. The man no longer appears as a strong beast, but turns into liquid water and a tall tree; passions pour out, pleasures spill, beauty withers, and it drops from its petal to the ground more quickly than a flower when the erotic blasts of insolence blow upon it, withering in corruption before the afternoon arrives. For desire does and shapes and pretends all things, so that it may hide the true man. But the man who has the Word dwelling with him does not change; he is not reshaped; he bears the form of the Word, is made like God, is beautiful—not adorned with beauty. Beauty is the true reality, for God is that reality; and that man becomes God because he wills what God wills. Heraclitus spoke rightly: 'Men are gods, gods are men,' a revealed mystery: God in man, and man God, and the will of the Father carried out by the Mediator; for the Word is the common Mediator of both, Son of God and Savior of men, servant of God and Pedagogue of men (John 1:14; 1 Timothy 2:5).

Since the flesh is a slave, as Paul also testifies, how can anyone reasonably adorn the servant like a leader? For the apostle says that the fleshly nature is the form of a slave, speaking of the Lord: 'He emptied Himself, taking the form of a slave' (Philippians 2:7)—he calls the outer man a slave before the Lord became a slave and bore flesh. But the sympathetic God Himself freed the flesh from corruption and from the bitter, death-bearing slavery, and having removed corruption, He clothed it with incorruptibility, the adornment of immortality, making this flesh holy [and] placing upon it the ornament of eternity. There is also another beauty of human beings: love. 'For love,' according to the apostle, 'is patient, is kind, does not envy, does not boast, is not puffed up' (1 Corinthians 13:4). Boasting is the adornment of excess and uselessness, carrying that emphasis. Therefore he adds, 'it does not behave shamefully' (1 Corinthians 13:5); for what is foreign and contrary to nature is shameful. The artificial is foreign, which he explains clearly by saying, 'it does not seek what is not its own' (1 Corinthians 13:5); for truth calls its own what belongs to it, but love of beauty seeks what is foreign, existing outside God and the Word and love. And the Spirit testifies through Isaiah that the Lord Himself became unattractive in appearance: 'We saw Him, and He had no form or beauty, but His appearance was without honor, despised by men' (Isaiah 53:2-3). And who is better than the Lord? Yet it was not the imaginary beauty of the flesh, but the true beauty of both soul and body that He displayed—the beneficial beauty of the soul and the immortal beauty of the flesh.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex tripartite psychology and the theological distinctions of the Greek text. Pass A and B both correctly handle the Heraclitus quote and the various Pauline and Isaianic citations. Pass B provides necessary scripture citations (Philippians 2:7, 1 Corinthians 13:4-5, Isaiah 53:2-3) which are required for clarity and match the Greek content. The translation of 'πρὶν ἢ τὸ μετόπωρον ἐλθεῖν' as 'before the afternoon comes' (Pass A) and 'before the afternoon arrives' (Pass B) is a valid rendering of the metaphorical sense of the text.
